en: The śramaṇa Zhizhou composed this treatise.
Regarding these falsely grasped [entities] up to their intrinsic natures (svabhāva) and specific differences (viśeṣa):

if one asks how the intrinsic nature and specific difference of the "self" are to be understood among the categories of phenomena, the answer is that the mere general designation of "self" is what is called its intrinsic nature.
Nature, pervasiveness, permanence, and so forth— these distinctions are termed "differentiation.
One should understand that this applies equally to [the self as] being distinct from the aggregates and so on.
This is also why it is said that "I" is the self-nature, the distinction, and so forth.
As for the statement in the treatise, "Because all appear as the grasped and the grasper":

Question: How is it known that both the semblance of the apprehended (*grāhya*) and the apprehender (*grāhaka*) are termed "clinging" (*abhiniveśa*)? Answer: The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha-bhāṣya* (Commentary on the Compendium of the Great Vehicle), Chapter Four, states:

"The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises based upon karma, afflictions, the apprehended, the apprehender, and the pervasive conceptualization of recollection (*parikalpita-anusmaraṇa*). It further states: "As previously explained, the false discrimination (*abhūta-parikalpa*) regarding the body and so forth—the apprehended and the apprehender of the various consciousnesses—is established as its nature. And it further states: "For example, like the mirage of a deer, by the power of its own continuity, it is established as resembling water."
The nature of false conceptualization regarding the grasped (grāhya) and the grasper (grāhaka) should be known as the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva).

By this, it is understood that both modes of grasping are termed "clinging" (abhiniveśa). Question: Are these two aspects of what is clung to simultaneous or not? Answer: There is an interpretation that this passage is general in scope.
In reality, whenever the mind clings to the grasper, the characteristic of the grasper exists;
the same applies to the grasped.
This is because one does not cling to these two at all times.
Treatise:
Regarding the statement that the *ālaya-vijñāna* serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*), the question is:
what is being proven by this? The answer is that there are two interpretations according to some authorities.
First, it is proven that the seven contaminated consciousnesses (*sāsrava-vijñāna*) which act as perfumers (*vāsaka*) all possess grasping (*sagraha*).

Second, it is generally proven that all eight [consciousnesses] are so, because it is said that the causes which produce them all possess grasping. Question: According to this master, is it admitted that the sixth consciousness possesses two types of grasping?
Regarding the two types of grasping, both are absent. Answer: There are two interpretations.
One says they are the same as Dharmapāla;
the other says they do not coexist.
As with the seventh [consciousness], because it lacks the grasping at phenomena as a self (*dharmanairātmya*).
Regarding the treatise’s statement that "imaginative discrimination (*vikalpa*) is able to universally conceptualize (*parikalpayati*)," [it means that]...
This is consistent with what is taught in Asaṅga’s *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*.
In his commentary, Vasubandhu states:
"One should know that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is capable of universal conceptualization (*parikalpa*) because it possesses discrimination (*savikalpa*)."
"Because it is intermingled with manifesting and recollective conceptualization. The commentary explains:
"Intermingled" means associated and co-arising.
Because the mental consciousness is accompanied by these two types of conceptualization, it is able to conceptualize.
"Manifestation" (*vijñapti*) is a synonym for "conceptualization" (*vikalpa*);

it is also termed "discernment" (*vicāra*). Regarding the statement that "it takes the seeds of the habitual tendencies of its own linguistic expressions as its cause": this means that the seeds of the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) from all consciousnesses throughout beginningless saṃsāra serve as the generative cause for this [manifestation].

Commentary: This explains that the seeds of the habitual tendencies of the discursive proliferation of all mental consciousnesses throughout beginningless birth and death act as the causal basis for the arising of this [manifesting consciousness].
This reveals that the seeds perfumed by one's own seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) constitute the substantial cause that directly produces one's own manifest activity (*pravṛtti*).
As for the treatises stating that all consciousnesses take the verbal designation-perfuming (*nāma-vikalpa-vāsanā*) as their seeds, [this refers to the seeds of the other-dependent nature].

This means that because it arises resembling those [objects]—having as its cause the seeds of the linguistic habit-energies (*nāma-vāsanā*) of the consciousnesses of infinite forms and so forth—it therefore proceeds as a conceptualization of all infinite aspects. Commentary:

When seeds are perfumed within the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) by means of the eighteen spheres (*dhātu*) and other consciousnesses, this is collectively termed "using another. By virtue of this,
the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises appearing as all things.
Therefore, it functions with infinite modes of activity (*ākāra*).
This is not something that the five or eight consciousnesses can possess.
[Treatise]
Regarding the statement, "Those who maintain that the grasping of self and dharmas must necessarily be wisdom (prajñā)":
[The opponent] asks, "If the five consciousnesses (pañca-vijñāna) can coexist with wisdom according to the Dharma-protectors (Dharmatrāta),
then by now challenging them, are you not biting your own finger?"
The answer is that there are two interpretations of this meaning.
The first says: because the five consciousnesses lack superior wisdom (*prajñā*), they are inferior and thus cannot grasp [the object].
The second says: this reason only challenges the eighth consciousness. A detailed examination states:
Now, wherever there is grasping (*upādāna*), there must necessarily be a concomitant sense of "mine" (*parigraha*).
This does not mean that all instances of "mine" are necessarily grasping;
for it is admitted that all contaminated minds (*sāsrava-citta*) involve grasping.
Therefore, it is difficult to provide a definitive explanation.
Thus, these two interpretations do not constitute a sound exposition.
Nevertheless, one may attain awakening by not departing from what is difficult to conceive.
Commentary:
According to the *Viṃśatikā*, up to the point where it says "there is also attachment to phenomena" (*dharmagrāha*),
the *Viṃśatikā-vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* clarifies that the knowledge of others' minds (*paracittajñāna*) is both tainted (*sāsrava*) and untainted (*anāsrava*).
Regarding the explanation of that untainted knowledge of others' minds (*anāsrava-paracittajñāna*), there are three points.
First, one master interprets that the essence of that bodhisattva’s untainted knowledge of others' minds also possesses attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*).
The treatise states: "Not knowing as the Buddha knows" clearly indicates the presence of grasping;
"not knowing" is precisely the meaning of ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Because that ignorance has not yet been severed and it obscures the mind, one does not accord with the Buddha.
Commentary:
Regarding the meaning of the verse by Master Ānanda,
according to that sutra it says:
If ignorance and the various views were of a single characteristic, there would be no cultivation or liberation;
the ordinary person and the Buddha would not be distinct. Why is this so?
Because the afflictions are of one and the same essential nature. Why is this?
Because they arise and cease simultaneously within a single mind, being neither distinct nor different from one another.
O Son of the Buddha, if one who is bound could understand the single characteristic [of liberation],
then the four great elements could become one,
and the six flavors would not differ.
Because they are so greatly different, bondage and liberation are likewise.
O Son of the Buddha, when all bodhisattvas were ordinary beings,
they were fully possessed of all fetters.
Furthermore, when [afflictions] are severed, the coarse portions are eliminated first and the subtle portions are removed later.
If the affliction within a single moment of mind were a single entity,
there should not be the duality of light and darkness.
O Son of the Buddha, one may further infer the distant from the near:
if even in the wholesome minds of ordinary worldlings there is no unwholesomeness,
how much less could there be ignorance within the mind that is signless?
"O Son of the Buddha, to speak of 'good and evil as one mind' refers to the verse of the non-Buddhist teacher Andha in the kingdom of King Bimbisāra,
which clarifies that light and darkness share a single characteristic, and good and evil are one mind."
Regarding the treatise:
although there are two categories within the *Vijñānakāya*, it is said "this and that" because they reach [the full extent of the analysis].
These various distinctions, as indicated by the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*) and explained extensively in the treatises, cannot be recorded in their entirety here.
Now, I shall briefly list them according to what is required.
Regarding the two types of pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpa*) among the seventy-three [mental factors],
that treatise states:
The undifferentiated refers to all names universally conceptualized for all phenomena.
The differentiated refers to the various specific names universally conceptualized for these phenomena, such as "form" and so forth.

The commentary explains that because all names are reckoned as being substantially existent, they are said to be without distinction. Furthermore, regarding "the grasping of preparatory application" and so forth:
first, there are five types of grasping of preparatory application.
"Attachment, aversion, union, separation, and equanimity. The commentary states:
"By means of these preparatory applications (*prayoga*), grasping arises.
Attachment and aversion are, respectively, the two preparatory applications for union and separation."
The second is called the grasping at designations, which is further divided into two types:
that which is not produced by letters and that which is produced by letters.
That which is not produced by letters is as follows:
This refers to grasping at things by thinking, "What is this? How is this thing? What is this thing? How is this thing?
Regarding that which is produced by letters, it refers to grasping at things by thinking, "This is this thing; this thing is thus."
This refers to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the three natures (*tri-svabhāva*), the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and so forth;
this is consistent with the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*.

Furthermore, regarding "the differentiation of its own essence" and so forth, these shall be clarified in terms of their mutual inclusion within the eight types of differentiation. Furthermore, regarding "conformable awakening" and so forth:
The commentary states:
"In order, the manifest and the seeds are the objects imagined by the mind that performs universal imagination. Furthermore, according to [the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*] 73:
Regarding the four distinctions, such as the "clinging to self-nature" (*svabhāva-grāha*) and so forth: 1.

To conceive of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena within the three categories [of aggregates, bases, and elements] is called "clinging to self-nature. 2. To conceive of all phenomena, such as form (*rūpa*), according to their various modes of differentiation—such as being visible or invisible, outflowing (*sāsrava*) or non-outflowing (*anāsrava*), and so on—is called "clinging to differentiation" (*viśeṣa-grāha*). 3. To conceive of all phenomena, such as form, as being those respective objects of the mind and mental factors belonging to the three realms, the three natures, the outflowing and non-outflowing, and so forth, is called "clinging to the grasped" (*grāhya-grāha*). 4. To conceive of form and so forth as the grasper (*grāhaka*) of form and so forth is [the clinging to the grasper].
Furthermore, the reckoning of the mind and the mental factors (*caitta*)—the various phenomena that can be grasped by them—is called the "reckoning of the grasper" (*grāhaka-parikalpa*).
Moreover, regarding the phrase "reckoning the object based on the name" and so forth, according to the fifth fascicle of Vasubandhu’s *Mahāyānasaṃgrahabhāṣya*, it says:
First, the imagined nature of objects based on names,
which means that such-and-such a name has such-and-such an object.
Second, the imagined nature of names based on objects.
This means that such an object has such a name.
Third is the pervasive conceptualization of the intrinsic nature of names based on names;
this refers to the pervasive conceptualization of names whose referents have not yet been understood. Commentary:
This means that while one has understood the name but not yet understood the object, one clings to the name as being real.
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi* says:
"That is, failing to understand the object of form, one discriminates the name of form."
Fourth, the imagined nature of objects based on objects:
this refers to the conceptualization of objects whose names have not yet been understood.
Fifth, the imagined nature of both based on both: [this refers to the conceptualization of both names and objects].

This refers to the pervasive conceptualization of this name and this object as having such an essential nature (*svabhāva*). Furthermore, regarding the fivefold distinctions of the seven types of conceptualized objects and essential natures, the first is the "essential nature of the object" (*artha-svabhāva*).
There are four distinctions;
these are precisely the four types previously cited, namely the grasper, the grasped, and so forth.
Second is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This refers precisely to the two names previously cited: "differentiated" and "undifferentiated.
Third is the defiled self-nature, which means reckoning this form as possessing greed, hatred, and delusion.
One cannot distance oneself from the fetters of greed, hatred, and delusion;
furthermore, one is not endowed with any wholesome qualities.
The same applies to the calculation of the remaining aggregates and so forth.
One should understand that the four purities are the reverse of defilement.
The fifth is neither defiled nor pure;

it is merely the conceptualization of all phenomena as grasper and grasped. Furthermore, this is the fifth preparatory stage (*prayoga*) from the sixteenth chapter of the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
This refers precisely to the two aforementioned preparatory stages (*prayoga*).
Regarding the six [factors] such as non-text (*a-vyañjana*) and so forth, they are likewise the same as the two aforementioned [stages];
therefore, they are not cited again. Furthermore, according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 36, and other sections:

Regarding the eight types of discrimination: the discrimination of the various intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of form and so forth is called "discrimination of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāva-vikalpa*). The discrimination of all principles concerning form and so forth—such as being visible or invisible, the three natures, the three realms, the three periods of time, and their opposites—is called "discrimination of distinctions" (*viśeṣa-vikalpa*). To grasp collectively all phenomena, whether sentient or insentient, as being either provisional or real, is [the discrimination of totalization].
The conceptualization arising from causes is called "conceptualization of grasping at a whole," because it grasps the five aggregates and so forth as a self and what belongs to a self;
thus, it is called the two types of conceptualization: "self" and "what belongs to a self. It takes as its object various pure, excellent, and agreeable realms.

The conceptualization that arises is called "conceptualization of the agreeable. Conceptualization arising in dependence on objects that are impure and disagreeable is called "conceptualization of the disagreeable. Conceptualization produced in dependence on objects that are both pure and impure, or both agreeable and disagreeable—which are neutral—is called "conceptualization of the contrary-to-both. These give rise to the three types of entities.
The first three types of discrimination give rise to the first matter;
the next two types of discrimination give rise to the second matter;
and the final three types of discrimination give rise to the third matter. Furthermore, regarding the ten types of discrimination in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts, the commentary states:

"Discrimination" (*vikalpa*) refers to that which is capable of discriminating; among the ten [categories] of the Abhidharma, both the object and the subject of discrimination are termed "discrimination.
This is as reconciled in that commentary (*śāstra*). According to Asvabhāva, it says:
This means that the ālayavijñāna is the root of all other forms of conceptualization (*vikalpa*);
since its own nature is also conceptualization, it is likewise called the "root.
As for "conceptualization of the characteristics of objects":
This refers to the conceptualization that form and so forth possess such-and-such characteristics.
Regarding "conceptualization of the manifestation of characteristics":

this means that the visual consciousness and other [sensory consciousnesses], together with their respective supporting consciousnesses, manifest as if resembling the characteristics of those objects of perception. Commentary:
The "consciousnesses of the eye and so forth" include the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).
The "consciousness that serves as their support" refers to the *manas*.

The fact that the six evolving consciousnesses can manifest images resembling their respective objects is called the "manifestation of the aspect. Regarding the "discrimination of the transformation of the objective aspect":
This refers to the discrimination arising from the transformation of consciousness that resembles reflections such as form and so forth. The commentary states:
it is precisely the appearance of the object of cognition (*ālambana-nimitta*) that undergoes transformation;
the discriminating subject (*grāhaka-vikalpa*) is named after that [object].
That is to say, old age, illness, the three types of sensation, and greed, hatred, and delusion serve as the conditions for transformation,
causing the physical form and color of the body to undergo change.
The substance of this transformation is precisely the material body and so forth.
Regarding the statement that "because of pleasure, the face is serene and so forth," this clarifies the conceptualization of the transformation of characteristics;
that is to say, by means of the supporting faculties such as the eye,
the images of forms and so forth are made to appear.
The various transformations of visual consciousness and the other consciousnesses give rise to conceptual constructions within them,
just as the aforementioned transformations such as aging were explained. [Commentary:]
Due to the transformation of the supporting body— the sense faculties and so forth—
the supported consciousness also undergoes transformation,
manifesting the forms of the five sensory objects.
"Intentionally" refers to the consciousness that is capable of objective apprehension and conceptualization.
The mention of "aging and so forth" indicates that the conditions for transformation are the same as those previously mentioned.
The remainder may be understood from the textual characteristics cited in the commentary. Furthermore, in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, there are ten types of mental distraction (*vikṣepa*).
First, the signless;
second, the sign-possessing;
third, the superimposed.
Fourth, destruction;
fifth, identity;
sixth, difference.
Seventh, self-nature;
eighth, differentiation;
ninth, apprehending an object according to its name.
The ten aspects of "suchness" (tathatā) are termed conceptual distractions (*vikalpa*).
To counteract these ten types of distraction, non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*) is taught throughout all the *Prajñāpāramitā* scriptures. Commentary:

Scattered movement (*vikṣepa*) is simply another name for conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, regarding the twelve [types of] views mentioned in the *Abhidharma*, the ten [views] that are neither "view" nor "non-view" are subsumed within the twenty-eight views.
For this reason, I have not cited it here. Furthermore, regarding the seventy-seven [points] which possess ten characteristics,
those that are excluded by the eighteen emptinesses are explained in great detail in that treatise.
Now, to quote briefly:
there are ten kinds of signs that emptiness can eliminate.
First, the sign of perceiving the meaning of phenomena as having letters.

1. The emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*) correctly eliminates the characteristic of the continuous evolution of arising and ceasing, because one understands that the meaning of *tathatā* (suchness) is established as twofold. 2.

The emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the prior and posterior (*pūrvāpara-śūnyatā*) correctly eliminate [the characteristic of] attachment to the body and the characteristic of the conceit of "I" (*asmimāna*), because one understands the grasper (*grāhaka*). 3. One understands the grasper as having attachment to the body and the characteristic of the conceit of "I."

This is dispelled by internal emptiness (*adhyātma-śūnyatā*) and the emptiness of the non-apprehendable (*anupalambha-śūnyatā*). Fourth, the perception of the apprehended object as having the characteristic of being concerned with wealth is dispelled by external emptiness (*bahirdhā-śūnyatā*). Fifth, the perception of the apprehended object as having the characteristic of internal bliss and external excellence associated with the enjoyment of women, male attendants, and material requisites [is dispelled by the emptiness of both].

1. It is eliminated by the emptiness of internal and external phenomena and by the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*). 2. Having realized the establishment of the six [perfections], there is the sign of the immeasurable;

this is eliminated by the emptiness of the great (*mahā-śūnyatā*). 3. Having realized that the formless realm possesses the sign of internal tranquility and liberation, there is the emptiness of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). 4. Because one realizes the suchness of signs, there is the sign of the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and phenomena—as well as the sign of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of consciousness.

Ultimate non-substantiality, the self-nature of non-substantiality, and the emptiness of the ultimate are able to correctly eliminate [the misconceptions regarding] the ninth [point]: that the perfectly pure *tathatā* (suchness) possesses the characteristics of being unconditioned and immutable.
The two types of emptiness—unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and unchanging (*avikāra*)—are eliminated [by the emptiness of emptiness].
Tenth, regarding the emptiness that serves as the antidote to those [two], one attends to and contemplates the characteristic of the emptiness of emptiness;
this is correctly eliminated by the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*). Furthermore, the twelfth [point] follows the fourth chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, which states:

This refers to being attached to various kinds of speech, exquisite sounds, and verbal designations; it refers to engaging in such reflection as thinking that there must exist the characteristics of real entities corresponding to those prior phenomena.
The noble one’s cultivation of practice consists in knowing that speech arises in dependence upon those dharmas; this is called the discrimination of the knowable.

That is to say, within the very sphere of the knowable, the grasping at various characteristics—such as heat, moisture, motion, and solidity—as being real is called the discrimination of names and signs. The conceptualization of names and meanings refers to the various real spheres of objects, such as gold and silver, which are taken as the referents of names. The discrimination of self-nature and form refers to the focused recollection of the intrinsic essence and the specific characteristics of existing phenomena.
This dharma is thus and not otherwise; it is not a vision of right view, but is called the discrimination of self-nature. That is to say:
by whatever causes and by whatever conditions.

The conceptualization of causes refers to the arising of the perception of distinct objects due to the causal characteristics of existence and non-existence. The conceptualization of views refers to the clinging and discrimination of non-Buddhist outsiders who hold false views such as existence, non-existence, identity, difference, both, or neither. The conceptualization of establishment refers to the proclamation of false dharmas by grasping at the signs of "self" and "what belongs to self. The conceptualization of production refers to the arising of a mind of attachment toward the existence or non-existence of things based on various conditions. [It is said that] all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen.

Because they are originally non-existent, yet exist by depending on causes and conditions, the absence of the names "cause" and "effect" is called the discrimination of non-arising. This refers to the conjunction of various dharmas, such as gold and thread combined together.
What are the phenomena that, when combined, are called "discrimination of combination"? This refers to the attachment to the causes of bondage, just as one who is bound.
It is like a person who uses skillful means to tie a knot in a rope; having tied it, he then unties it—this is called the discrimination of "bondage and non-bondage."
O Mahāmati, this is called the characteristic of the differentiation of the essence of dharmas through false discrimination. Furthermore, regarding the sixteenth:
that which is eliminated by the sixteen kinds of emptiness—since emptiness is capable of eliminating [them].
The number of phenomena to be eliminated is likewise the same;
that which is eliminated is precisely the conceptualized phenomena (*vikalpa-dharma*).
All subsequent mentions of "that which is eliminated" should be understood according to this principle. Furthermore, regarding the twenty-eight views (*dṛṣṭi*):
This is explained in detail in the Abhidharma treatises;
here, I shall speak briefly.
First, regarding "viewing characteristics": this refers to hearing the Mahāyāna teachings on emptiness that convey the profound intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).

To cling to such characteristics as the non-existence of the [three] natures is called the view of characteristics; because of this, one slanders the Buddha’s teaching on the three natures, thereby giving rise to a second view:
the view that destroys conventional designations.
Third, the destruction of the view of conceptualization;
fourth, the destruction of the view of reality. Furthermore, because he wishes to establish this false view, he collects a few principles based on sūtras of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
They employ skillful means to transform [the teachings] so that they accord with their own views;

for this reason, they further give rise to the five views of appropriation and the sixth view of transformation. Furthermore, based on these views, they give rise to the attachment that whether one performs wholesome or unwholesome deeds according to these views, there is no fault whatsoever.

Having attained liberation from all obscurations and defilements, they further give rise to seven views of non-offense and eight views of renunciation. Having become attached to their own views, they disparage, revile, and harbor malice toward the Śrāvaka Piṭaka and the Śrāvakas.

Furthermore, they give rise to a ninth view, the view of disparagement, and a tenth view, the view of indignation. Moreover, in accordance with their own evil views, they perversely establish emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
Furthermore, they consider that all the dharmas they have established for their own awakening and for the awakening of others will all produce immeasurable merit.
Furthermore, they give rise to eleven inverted views and twelve views of origination; thus, by means of reasoning, they refute what has been established,
fail to establish their own tenets,
and frivolously employ fallacious reasoning to refute others.
Furthermore, they give rise to thirteen views that do not establish a tenet and the fourteenth, the view of arrogance and confusion.
They also give rise to a conceited mind, claiming that practicing in this way is the true offering and veneration of all Buddhas.

This is the fifteenth, called "the view of reverent service. Furthermore, the discerning observer causes others to abandon evil views by employing skillful means based on the principles of reality to awaken them, never harboring a mind of rejection.
That is to say, this alone is true while all others are false and delusive;

this is called the sixteenth, the stubbornly ignorant view. The aforementioned habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*) of these views are called the seventeenth, the fundamental view. The eighteenth is the view of non-view regarding views, which is precisely the characteristic of the aforementioned views.

This is because one truly and firmly clings to such characteristics as non-existence and so forth, yet gives rise to the perception that does not cling to any characteristics whatsoever. (19) The abandonment of the view of expedient means refers to the aforementioned three views: the view of deprecation regarding designations, conceptual constructions, and reality.
Because one conceives of all dharmas as arrogant and gives rise to the notion that diligent effort is useless, there is the twentieth, the view of non-transcendence;
this consists of the two aforementioned views of grasping and transformation.
Because practicing without skillful means does not lead to the realization of the fruit;

twenty-first, the view of the increase [of faults], which consists of the aforementioned two views of being without fault and of renunciation, because one's conduct is deviant and there is no possibility of exhausting the obstacles; twenty-second, the view that produces non-merit.

That is to say, the two views of disparagement and resentment previously mentioned give rise to misconduct toward the True Dharma and those of the same holy life; through this gateway, they cause great harm. (23) The view of fruitlessness.
That is to say, the aforementioned perversions give rise to two views.

Because the established doctrine cannot be realized as a superior fruit by either the teacher or the recipient, [the first] is the twenty-fourth view, the view of humiliation (*avamanyanā-dṛṣṭi*). This refers to the two views of pride (*mada*) and confusion (*saṃkara*), which do not establish a formal thesis.
25. The view of slanderous criticism (*abhyākhyāna-dṛṣṭi*): because one who engages in irrational debate cannot possibly achieve victory;

this refers to the aforementioned view of honoring [wrong teachers], for it involves forcibly attributing qualities that should not be predicated. 26. The view of being unfit for conversation (*asambhāṣya-dṛṣṭi*).
This refers to the aforementioned stubborn and deluded views;
one should not speak with those who falsely cling to emptiness, for speaking with them is of no benefit. Twenty-seven: Vast Views.
This refers to the aforementioned fundamental view (*mūladṛṣṭi*).
Because it causes evil views to increase and expand in the future, there is the twenty-eighth, the view of overweening pride (*abhimānadṛṣṭi*).
The preceding twenty-seven views are all termed "overweening" (*abhimāna*).
Furthermore, it is because one can give rise to false and unsubstantial overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Regarding the statement in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* that "it is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) and so forth," [the commentary states:]...
According to that treatise:
"If the nature of the thoroughly imagined (parikalpita-svabhāva) depends upon the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva), it does not exist in reality."
Regarding the phrase "appearing as an object," it is further stated that the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature) is called the "object of universal conceptualization" (*parikalpya*).
As for the commentary's question, "If it does not face the mind, how should it be known?"— this refers to the following.
Question: What teaching should be known as the proof? Answer: The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, states:
Question: Of the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), how many should be thoroughly known (*parijñeya*)?
Answer: All of them.
Therefore, it is known that the thoroughly imagined nature is also an object of knowledge (*jñeya-dharma*).
As for the statement in various holy teachings that "it extends to all that is grasped as an object of attachment":
According to the verse in the *Madhyāntavibhāga-bhāṣya*:
"Because neither duality nor existence nor non-existence exists,
it is neither existent nor non-existent."
"Neither different nor identical;
this is explained as the characteristic of emptiness. The prose commentary explains:
"Non-duality means the absence of the grasped and the grasper."
"Existence and non-existence" refers to the non-existence of the two types of grasping.
This reveals that emptiness has non-substantiality as its nature. The commentary states:
the emptiness of the two types of grasping is called "non-substantiality."

Because this nature is not non-existent, it is called "existence-non-existence. Regarding the statement in the *Treatise*, "Why is it not existence-non-existence? Because both exist," the commentary explains: one falsely clings to the duality of subject and object as being existent.
The absence of those two [grasps] is called "the existence of non-duality. The treatise asks: "How is it not non-existent? It states:
"Because the two absences exist. The commentary explains:

Because the principle of the two absences of self (*nairātmya*) is not non-existent, they are said to exist as the two absences. The treatise states: This emptiness and that false discrimination are neither different nor identical.
If they were different, it would follow that the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is distinct from the phenomena themselves,
which would contradict correct reasoning, as in the case of their generic similarity (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa).
If they were one, then it would not be an object of pure gnosis (viśuddha-jñāna).
Nor is it a common characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*). The commentary states:
It should not be said that the two emptinesses (*dvaya-śūnyatā*) are the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), because they would then be distinct from those phenomena.
If [the two] were one, it should not be said that the principle of the two emptinesses is the object of non-conceptual pure wisdom;
for it would be identical with the particular phenomenon (*vastu*).
(Commentary)
Regarding the statement that the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-division (*nimitta-bhāga*) each possess various modes of activity (*ākāra*),

"Within a single consciousness, one part undergoes transformation and appears as the semblance of the grasped object (*grāhya-nimitta*)."
One part transforms into the aspect resembling the grasper (*darśana-bhāga*).
These two parts each possess various distinct modes of appearance (*ākāra*) that arise simultaneously.
If one does not admit that a single consciousness can possess various aspects at one time, [this would be untenable].
There should not be a single moment of cognizing various objects.

As detailed in the commentary,
it is now difficult to explain [otherwise].
"The body" and "consciousness" refer to the *ālaya-vijñāna*.
That which is the support for this group of five consciousnesses is called the "body.
If that is so, since the sixth [consciousness] also relies upon the eighth, why is it said to rely on only five?

That treatise states:
"Because it appears through calculation across three periods. Answer: If one discusses the reflected image, it is indeed as you have criticized;
however, this commentary relies upon its original source.
They are likewise merely objective appearances;
therefore, only five are mentioned.

The essence of the good and evil destinies is, in reality, solely the retributive consciousness (*vipākavijñāna*);
since it is discussed in terms of both the grasped and the grasper, as well as the requisites and so forth,
the destinies are also [its] characteristics.

reflect upon this.

It is like a lamp.

This is because one follows others for the sake of protecting the meaning of the Dharma.

Regarding the explanation of two phrases as being "two":

The fourth section, "Correcting the Conclusions," is precisely this passage.

Answer: Because Master Nanda’s two-part conclusion regarding the dependent nature (*paratantra*) accords with that [system], and he does not mention self-cognition (*svasaṃvitti*) or the cognition of self-cognition (*svasaṃvittisaṃvitti*).
The *Shao tong hufa* (Lesser Treatise on Protecting the Dharma) states that [the first master] was already [refuted] by others, and thus it is called the "first master's knot.

The preceding [text] clarifies its own position, stating that there are four knots because they are correct; therefore, there is no contradiction. Alternatively, the character "first" (*chū*) may be an error and should be "later" (*kō*).
This indicates that this concluding phrase was not composed by Sthiramati;
since it applies to both meanings, one should follow the majority of the manuscripts.
Thus says the treatise.

Regarding the phrase "excluding the particular and universal characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), space (*ākāśa*), and so forth," one commentary states: "The universal characteristic is as explained in the *Hetuvidyā* (Logic).
Since it lacks a distinct substantial nature (*svabhāva*) and cannot be said to be permanent, the word 'permanent' serves to exclude it."
Now, regarding this reliance on the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* to explain suffering, impermanence,

and so forth: there is an interpretation that although the universal characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) may be called "pervasive," it is not termed "accomplished" because it is subject to arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, as stated in the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*, the "common characteristic" (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) merely negates the unmanifest (*avijñapti*).
Characteristics such as suffering and impermanence possess both negation and affirmation.
Because the former lacks intrinsic nature and the latter arises and ceases, neither can be permanent.
"All" serves as a restrictive exclusion. The detailed commentary states:
The *Śāstra* contains no explicit text definitively establishing that [the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*] relies on the *Nyāyapraveśa* rather than the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra*.
Nevertheless, it says that the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) observed by the mind have no substantial reality.
Furthermore, regarding the *Śāstra*’s explanation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), selflessness (*anātman*), the two types of suffering (*duḥkha*), and the two types of impermanence (*anitya*):
because these are treated as equivalent in the treatise, the commentary (*ṭīkā*) does not explain them; they are omitted following the treatise.
This does not mean that those [categories] are not admitted to be included among what is being excluded.
This universally excludes the "common characteristics" (sāmānya-lakṣaṇa) as explained in both the sūtras and the śāstras.
If you say that it only excludes the common characteristics mentioned in the sūtras,
for what reason does it not exclude those mentioned in the śāstras?
How could it be argued that the universal characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) is not excluded?
If it were not excluded, there would be the fault of incomplete exclusion since the universal characteristic is constantly being excluded;
therefore, there is no contradiction with the Commentary.
There is an interpretation that this is insufficient.
The Commentary states: "Because that which is universally conceptualized does not exist in such a manner."
This is a brief citation.
It should be stated as follows: "Because that which is thoroughly imagined never exists in such a manner.
The commentary says:
What exists conventionally is merely the result of deluded conceptualization regarding existence;
these things are eternally non-existent and are called the "perfectly established nature" (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).
Commentary.
Regarding this "separation from what was previously associated":
previously, it was the mind capable of producing and capable of conceptualizing that was termed "imagining" (parikalpa);
here, it is that which serves as the basis for what is conceptually grasped (parikalpita-svabhāva) that is termed "imagining."
Commentary:
Furthermore, the passage from "the dependent nature" up to "is called the thoroughly imagined nature" is identical to Vasubandhu’s later explanation.
Commentary:
Regarding the statement, "That which is said to be the object of the parikalpita (imagined) nature," that refers to the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*).
Question: According to the two bodhisattvas, the basis for the *parikalpita* is the dependent designation (*upādāya-prajñapti*) based upon the *paratantra* (dependent nature).
Yet, you claim that by stating they are "not different," one explains the root treatise.

If one does not rely on the provisional statement that the two natures are mutually related to explain the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra*, then the principle that they are neither separate nor non-separate can likewise be established.
As for the statement in the *Mūla-śāstra*:
"Because it is the characteristic of the object of the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*)," the commentary explains:
"Because the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) can give rise to the sixth consciousness, which is the mind of pervasive conceptualization."
If there were no such objects of dependence (paratantra), the grasping at a real self, dharmas, and so forth,
which are distinct from consciousness, would not arise.
If one is able to realize that [the object] does not arise, what could there be to be grasped as the nature of pervasive conceptualization?
For this reason, because of these two natures, they are not different.
It is just like the perception of a snake arising only when there is a rope.
The rest may be understood by analogy.
Regarding the treatise’s statement, "Just as magical illusions, etc., are non-existent yet appear to exist," and so forth:
The *Abhisamayālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* by Asaṅga clarifies these similes as they are fully listed in the commentary (*ṭīkā*).
Now, the *Vyākhyā* by Vasubandhu should be cited here: the treatise states, "Regarding the simile of magical illusions..."
Just as there is no actual elephant, yet there is the objective sphere of an illusory elephant,
so too is the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva):
although the six sense-bases that take form and so forth as their objects do not exist [independently], [the dependent nature still arises].
"When one engages in conceptual construction (*parikalpa*), there appears what seems to be an object of perception (*ālambana*) consisting of the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*). Commentary:
Externally, the eight [objects] such as the sensory fields (*viṣaya*) are taken as substantially real;
internally, by means of the eight similes, these are shown to be the opposite—that is, empty—and thus there should be eight types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
The first of these proofs states:
"The six objects, such as form and so forth,
do not exist as ultimate realities."
It appears clearly as an object of discursive conceptualization,
like a magical illusion; however,
suchness is not an object within the sphere of activity of that discursive conceptual appearance.

Therefore, it constitutes a dissimilar instance (*vipakṣa*), because it is neither the subject that performs the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpaka*) nor the object that is pervasively conceptualized (*parikalpya*).
Consequently, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntika*). Furthermore, it is like a mirage when it is flickering.
In reality there is no water, yet there is the perception of water;
the external vessel-world is likewise so.
As the *Pramāṇa* says:
The external vessel-world is empty and not substantially existent,
because it can give rise to minds and mental factors that grasp at it as being real.
It is like a mirage;
since suchness is not the basis for the arising of grasping, there is no lack of definiteness.
Furthermore, it is like the collection of mind and mental factors arising during sleep in a dream, which is extremely dull and obscure.
Although there are no objective referents such as forms and so forth,
there is the experience of desirable and undesirable objects;
it is the same during the waking state.
The Pramāṇa states:
"The objects of desire in a dream are neither desirable nor undesirable;
they are empty and not substantially existent."
Because it is cherished by a mind of attachment and aversion,
it is like a dream; or like seeing one's own reflection in a mirror or similar surface,
yet thinking, "I am now seeing a distinct image."
Yet this reflection has no real existence whatsoever.

It is likewise with the arising of the fruit of a reflection, which takes as its condition the substantial nature of wholesome or unwholesome volitional karma from a state that is not in meditative equipoise.
The *Pramāṇa* states:
"The fruits of wholesome and unwholesome karma are empty and not substantially existent."
Because they appear based on conditions, they are like reflections. Furthermore, it is like various shadows arising when a shadow-maker obscures light;
likewise, within the meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), various consciousnesses evolve with respect to distinctions that lack any real objective referent. Commentary:
Just as when one dances with many bodily gestures within a light,
their shadow likewise does so; so too,
through the power of meditative concentration, various bodily actions arise through discernment, yet remain free from conceptual differentiation.
Just as a physical form obscures light, so does the body arise dependent upon consciousness;
therefore, that body is designated by the name "various consciousnesses.
Alternatively, because the concentrated mind in the two higher realms is not singular, it is called "various consciousnesses."
Since this consciousness arises in dependence upon an unreal object,
it is clear that the mind is empty.
Based on the previous formal argument (*pramāṇa*), it is stated:
The bodily actions arising from meditative concentration are empty and not substantially existent,
because they undergo various transformations,
just like reflections and shadows.
According to the subsequent authority, it is said:
"The various consciousnesses of the meditative states are empty and not substantially existent, because they arise based on various conditions, like shadows and reflections;
furthermore, like an echo, they have no actual sound."
Yet it causes the listener to seem to hear various verbal expressions and diverse realms of discourse;
the vocal karma is likewise. The formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows:
Verbal action is not real, because it is heard by the listener;
it is like an echo. Furthermore, it is like the moon in water: because of the water's moist, smooth, and clear nature, although there is no actual moon, the moon can be perceived.
The mental consciousness associated with all samādhis, which has as its nature being moistened and purified by the cultivation of objects that are real entities, is likewise such that,
although there is no object that is a real entity, it appears to function as if there were.
What is the difference between this and a reflected image?
There is a distinction based on whether one is in a state of meditative concentration (*samāhita*) or a non-concentrated state (*asamāhita*). The commentary states:
The object of meditative concentration can cause the continuum of wholesome factors to persist; this is what is called "the true meaning" (*bhūtārtha*).
Alternatively, it is said that by excluding the objects of the thoroughly imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), they are termed "valid cognitions" (*pramāṇa*).
The objects manifested in meditative concentration are empty and not truly existent.
It manifests based on pure conditions, just like the moon reflected in water; or again, it is like a transformation, which is called a "transformation" because it depends upon this [basis].
Although it lacks substantial reality, the one who performs the transformation does not fall into error and exerts diligent effort toward the object being transformed.
So too it is with the bodhisattva:
although there are no sentient beings that are conceptually imputed,
out of compassion for all classes of sentient beings who exist dependently, [the bodhisattva acts].
"And going to those various places of birth to assume a self-body. The commentary explains:
This means that based on this very mind capable of transformation (*nirmāṇa-citta*), one initiates transformative activities;
or, based on that which is transformed, one gives rise to the mind capable of transformation.
Although the name "birth in a realm without karma" lacks substantial reality,
the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) states:
Bodhisattvas undergo birth.
Emptiness is not a substantial reality;
it arises from a non-erroneous mind, just like a magical transformation. As the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā* states:
Regarding non-fluctuation and non-erroneousness:
this means knowing that objects are neither existent nor non-existent, like illusions and so forth,
because they do not fluctuate between existence and non-existence.
Regarding the use of metaphors such as illusions to illustrate the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), since the two treatises differ, what is the intent behind each?

Answer: The *Madhyāntavibhāga* (Distinction Between the Middle and the Extremes) relies upon the actual substance of those illusory phenomena, as well as the grasping mind and the grasped objects such as water, to serve as metaphors for both natures [the imagined and the dependent].
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* bases its analysis on phenomena alone, categorizing them as merely dependent;
therefore, there is no contradiction with the treatise.
Regarding the phrase "the true suchness of transmigration" and so forth,
the texts in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and this treatise differ;
these are reconciled as explained in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).
There is an interpretation that conditioned phenomena are of two kinds:
first, those transformed by the four characteristics and produced by causes and so forth;
second, those produced by afflictions.
Now, when it is said that "conditioned" is spoken of according to the latter sense,
the term "conditioned" refers solely to dependent origination;
this explanation is superior.
Because the following section subsumes [the factors] under two natures;
however, the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra* states:
"One contemplates the true nature of the flow and transformation of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) within both defiled and purified dharmas."
"According to worldly purity, there is no contradiction. To explain in detail:
it is not that this principle does not exist;

however, the subsequent summary states that as for inclusion according to characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), [the factors] of the flow of existence (*pravṛtti*) are included within the first two natures (*svabhāva*) of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*).
Since it is said to "follow the characteristics," it is clear that this does not contradict principle;
it is spoken of in terms of their predominance.
The *Xiányán* (Exposition of the Manifest) further states that regarding defiled and pure phenomena (*saṃkleśa-vyavadāna-dharma*),
it does not say that pure phenomena depend on worldly purity.
Based on this scriptural principle, there is no contradiction in the commentary’s explanation.

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the sub-commentary (ṭīkā) below, "The process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*) refers exclusively to that which is with-outflows (*sāsrava*)," this discusses the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, which elucidates transmigration.
The treatise states:
Regarding the four established *tathatās*:

Question: Since all four are established [as such], why is it discussed only in terms of suffering? Answer: Although they are designated by a general name, they are nonetheless established based on specific phenomena, just as in the case of the sense-base of form (*rūpāyatana*) and so forth.
Furthermore, among the Four Noble Truths, the first is designated by its general name,
while the latter three are established by their specific names because they follow after it.
Treatise.
This refers to certain instances where the five categories are not subsumed under the [three] natures.
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 74, it asks:
"Among the five dharmas of the first nature (*svabhāva*), how many are subsumed?"
Answer: None are included. Question:
By how many are the second intrinsic nature (svabhāva) included?
Answer: It is included by four.
Question: By how many [of the three natures] is the third nature subsumed?
Answer: It is subsumed by one.
Treatise:
Furthermore, regarding those instances that reach the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*),
according to the *Madhyāntavibhāga-kārikā*, it is said:
"The name is the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."
The characteristic, the discrimination, and the dependent;
suchness and correct gnosis—
these are subsumed within the perfected nature.
Commentary:
If the substance and the characteristic were mutually exclusive in their inclusion,
then [one would have to consider] the two substances of name and meaning as explained in the *Saṃgraha*.
If one were to subsume these five factors under the categories of name,
meaning, and substance, it would result in contradiction. Why is this so?
Among the five dharmas, "meaning" (artha) consists of the "imagined" (parikalpita) and the "discriminated" (vikalpita);
its "substance" (svabhāva) is the "dependent" (paratantra).
That meaning is the first nature (prathama-svabhāva).
Regarding the statement in the Commentary: "How could it not be contradictory for the non-apprehension [of the imagined nature] to include the existent [nature]?
and "The *Madhyāntavibhāga* includes the three natures within the ten realities," etc.:
That treatise explains their mutual inclusion extensively in its second chapter;
here, I shall merely cite their names and briefly clarify their intended meaning.
First is the fundamental reality (*mūla-tattva*).
Because the other realities are established based upon this, the reality of two aspects is established by means of the three natures;
for it is non-erroneous with respect to the characteristics of the fundamental reality.
Third is the reality free from inversion,
because it can counteract the four types of inversions— namely, the misconceptions of permanence, pleasure, self, and purity.
Fourth is the reality of cause and effect.
That is to say, the Four Noble Truths;
because there is a distinction between the causes and effects of defilement and purification.
Fifth, the coarse and subtle reality.
This refers to the distinction between the two: the conventional and the ultimate.
Sixth is the thoroughly established reality, which refers to what is thoroughly established through both worldly convention and logical reasoning.
Seventh is the reality of the domain of purified wisdom, which refers to the distinction between the domains of purified wisdom regarding the two obstacles: the afflictive and the cognitive.
Eighth is the reality of inclusion.
That is to say, the three natures (trisvabhāva) subsume the five categories (pañcavastu),
and the ninefold distinctions of reality (navavidha-tattva) subsume the seven suchnesses (saptatathatā) and the three natures.
The ten skillful truths:
one counteracts the ten views of self by cultivating the ten kinds of skillfulness regarding the aggregates and so forth.
(Commentary)

Regarding the statement, "Because the entirety of conceptualization is included within what is signified": Question: Since correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*), mind (*citta*), and so forth, pertain to both the signifier (*abhidhāna*) and the signified (*abhidheya*), why is conceptualization (*vikalpa*) considered exclusively the signified?

Answer: Within the category of the contaminated (*sāsrava*), there is a specific distinction made between characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), and conceptualization (*vikalpa*). It is in this sense that conceptualization is designated as the signified.
The reason why conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is exclusively that which is expressed (*vācya*) is that it is a contaminated synthesis;
therefore, correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*),
being singular, possesses both the capacity to express and that which is expressed.
According to one interpretation, the characteristic (lakṣaṇa) is exclusively that which is signified;
the name (nāman) is merely that which signifies;
and conceptualization (vikalpa) pertains to both.
Because there are differences according to what the two [types of names] transform into, although there are many explanations, the one about to be presented is superior. To examine this:
just as a name expresses its referent, is that which is expressed by the name not itself a name?
If it is a name, why is it not that which is expressed?
If names arise based on the transformation of consciousness, why are they not name-aspects (*nāma-nimitta*)?
If you grant that they are aspects, [then...]
The *nimitta* (image) is itself the signifier (*vācaka*).
If it is the case that consciousness is called a "signifier" because it can transform into a signifier,
then since the image follows from [consciousness], it should be called "discrimination" (*vikalpa*) alone, following its source in that which transforms.
Because they arise from what has been transformed, only the two—characteristic (*nimitta*) and name (*nāman*)—are [so designated].
Since this is not the case here, how could it be so there?
Therefore, the commentary is superior.
Now, I shall provide one interpretation:

the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*) are exclusively the signified (*vācya*); whereas names (*nāman*) pertain to both the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*).
Although they are called "transformations of consciousness" (vijñānapariṇāma), they are also mutually inclusive;
however, based on a specific sense, they are designated simply as "names" (nāman).
Were it not so, there would be the fault of following the same pattern as previously mentioned regarding the mutual inclusion of the "aspects" (nimitta).
This can be understood through reflection.
As for the statement in the *Śāstra* that it is also called "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and so forth:
According to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*,
it is also called the "thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita*) and also called the "formed through conjunction" (*sāṃyogika*).
It is also called the "characteristic of superimposition," also called "false conceptual grasping," and also called "that which is manifested by verbal expression."
It is also called the application of syllables;
it is also called mere sound;
it is also called that which lacks substantial essence or characteristics.
Commentary:
Therefore, when the fourth [category] mentions "clinging to the nature of the thoroughly imagined" (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and so forth,
it refers specifically to the fourth of the five matters, namely, clinging (*abhiniveśa*).
Commentary:
Regarding the four principles (*yukti*),

1. It serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) for the arising of the two types of grasping, and is thus called the "basis of grasping" (*grāhaka-āśraya*). 4. It can serve as the basis for the grasping of phenomena (*dharma-grāha*). 5.

This means that it serves as the objective support for the arising of the antidotes to the two kinds of fivefold activities. Furthermore, it says:

this is a question based on the citation of the sūtra.

yet, having realized perfect peace (*parinirvāṇa*) in person, why would there be no nirvana?

This treatise explains that within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), there is the intentional meaning (*samdhi*) that birth and death and nirvana are without distinction, based upon the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Because the dependent nature serves as the basis for both the imagined and the perfected natures,
the Buddha realizes that within the limit of that dependent nature, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are non-dual;

Because the essence is one while the two aspects are distinct, from the perspective of ultimate truth, saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are both distinct and non-distinct; it is solely with reference to their non-distinction that the term "intentional meaning" (saṃdhāya) is used. (論何以故). This indicates the beginning of a formal inquiry into the preceding statement regarding the intentional nature of the teaching on the identity of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.*

"Because the dependent nature constitutes saṃsāra through its imagined aspect, and constitutes nirvāṇa through its perfected aspect. The commentary explains:
Since the dependent nature is established as either saṃsāra or perfect quiescence (parinirvāṇa) based on the imagined and perfected aspects respectively.

Answer: Because one clings to the parikalpita, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) continues in succession, and thus saṃsāra is never severed.

second, the purified portion;
third, the portion consisting of both.
"With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) was this said? The commentary states:
This is a question based on the sūtra. Within the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) constitutes the defiled portion (*saṃkleśa-bhāga*).
The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is the pure portion;
that is, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) constitutes those two portions.
It is with this underlying intention (*saṃdhi*) that such a statement was made.
It is like the three things that can be found within a worldly deposit of gold and earth:
first, the earth element;
second, the soil.
Regarding the three types of gold:
within the earth element, soil is not substantially existent yet is perceptibly obtainable;
gold is substantially existent yet is not obtainable.
When burned by fire, the characteristic of earth does not appear, but the characteristic of gold manifests.
Consciousness is also like this:
when it has not yet been burned by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom.
Within this consciousness, all that appears as the false, universally imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva) manifests,
while the true, perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva) does not manifest.
When this consciousness is consumed by the fire of non-conceptual wisdom (nirvikalpa-jñāna), [the former ceases].
Within this consciousness, that which is the true perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) manifests,
while that which is the false imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not manifest.
Therefore, this consciousness of false discrimination, as the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), possesses those two parts.
Regarding the earth element within a deposit of gold and soil, the *Vyākhyā* states:
"The earth is a metaphor for the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*); the soil is a metaphor for the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*)."
The metaphor of gold represents the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Since the nature of consciousness-only (*vijñapti-mātratā*) is the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), both the imagined (*parikalpita*) and the perfected natures are aspects of this [dependent] nature. Furthermore, it is said that the Blessed One has in some places taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are eternal.
In some places it is said that all phenomena are impermanent;
in other places it is said that all phenomena are neither permanent nor impermanent.
With what underlying intention (*abhiprāya*) was this stated?
That is to say, the dependent nature (paratantra-svabhāva) is permanent in its aspect as the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva),
impermanent in its aspect as the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva),
and neither permanent nor impermanent by virtue of those two aspects. The Commentary states:
This means that the essence of the *paratantra-svabhāva*, which is *tathatā*, is eternal;
whereas the aspect of the *parikalpita-svabhāva* is impermanent.
Because this nature is eternally non-existent, it is termed "impermanent."
It is not that there is arising and ceasing which is called impermanence.
